text: pretty much every spacie has lost to a puff because of her tech trap on platforms, where she up-throws you and either does or doesn't up-air. if she guesses right, she gets a free low percent rest. if she guesses wrong it doesn't matter as it's very easy to react if you guessed wrong or not. there is a way to get rid of this 50-50 entirely, making it a very similar gimmick to ice climbers' down-throw ? down-air. it is possible on every stage, but for sake of explanation we're going to use battlefield since the timing is the easiest to explain. say you are at ~12% and puff up throws you on the platform. at the apex, or slightly after, when you begin falling, you input a tech in case she does not do an up-air. this is because of how tech-trapping works. you essentially want to input the tech as soon as you are able to. because of how early you input this tech, you are then able to sdi her up-air up in order to waste the rest of the frames in which you are tech trapped, and can then tech her up air as well. this means that there is no longer an easy missed tech for her to rest in this situation. puff is not able to rest your sdi up until higher percents where you should just focus on di'ing up-air properly anyway. in order to counter this puff has to read your tech with rest, or reaction tech-chase you with something else. this setup should no longer be a free 50-50.

h2: Common Noob Habits to Break - NMW
preview: This is a list of problems that newer players consistently have. The list isn't comprehensive, but if you've been playing for less than 2 years, odds are you have at least a couple of these habits. If...
text: this is a list of problems that newer players consistently have. the list isn't comprehensive, but if you've been playing for less than 2 years, odds are you have at least a couple of these habits. if you can possibly watch footage of yourself, review it and note any of these habits. if you can't watch yourself, then just try to think about these things next time you play.

h2: Common Noob Habits to Break - NMW
preview: Using your jump as soon as you get out of hitstun in the air - This is extremely predictable and gives your opponent a free punish · Recovering by jumping and attacking instead of jumping to the ledge...
text: using your jump as soon as you get out of hitstun in the air - this is extremely predictable and gives your opponent a free punish recovering by jumping and attacking instead of jumping to the ledge - going high with an attack is almost always worse than sweetspotting ledge only recovering in one way - mix up your recovery options or you'll get read every time watching yourself getting comboed instead of trying to get out - always be looking for di mixups and escape options consistently doing survival di instead of combo di - know when to di to survive vs when to di to escape combos attacking when cornered - often it's better to focus on escaping rather than throwing out moves mindless full hops when cornered - full hopping in corner is extremely punishable excessive rolling - rolling is predictable and easily punished, especially when done repeatedly excessive spot dodges - spot dodge has long endlag and is easy to bait and punish excessive shield grabs - shield grab is slow and doesn't work against spaced moves not respecting crouch cancel - at low percents, many moves get cc punished. adjust your approach teching in place too much - tech in place is the easiest option to cover, mix it up tech rolling toward the center of the stage too much - this is extremely common and easily read. note: tech rolling toward center is common, but tech rolling away is rare (less than 5 noobs do this consistently vs 200+ who tech roll in) grabbing the ledge indiscriminately when ledgeguarding from the stage is better - sometimes staying on stage gives you better coverage spamming ledgehop aerials, especially dair with spacies - this is predictable and often gets you killed spamming finishing moves in neutral instead of combo starters - use moves that lead to combos, not just kill moves going for hard reads when you don't have a read - don't commit to risky options without reason going for a read in a reactable situation - if you can react to it, don't guess pointless movement, usually involving wavelands and platforms - just because you can do a movement trick doesn't mean you should. against marth, for example, it's hardly ever actually a good idea to go to platforms trying to use moves that are just bad - some moves have very limited utility, don't force them spamming an option because it works and not because it's good (specifically in friendlies) - this develops bad habits that won't work against better players trying to do too many things - master specific setups and gradually build up your arsenal. don't try to learn everything at once watch footage of yourself and actively look for these patterns focus on breaking 1-2 habits at a time, not all of them at once ask better players to call you out when they see these habits be conscious of these habits during play and actively work against them remember: these habits are so common that good players specifically look for and punish them

h3: Ego and Arrogance: Difficulty Taking Feedback
preview: With ego comes arrogance, which results in difficulty taking feedback · It can be hard to listen to someone who is way worse than you talk about the game · We should make sure we don't neglect informa...
text: with ego comes arrogance, which results in difficulty taking feedback it can be hard to listen to someone who is way worse than you talk about the game we should make sure we don't neglect information about the game because it comes from an unexpected source example: top players have been told for years that powershielding doesn't reduce shieldstun - melee is full of mysterious mechanics and no one knows everything more commonly, ego makes us unable to take criticism about our gameplay sometimes players worse than you can notice bad habits or deficiencies that aren't obvious to you ego might even be what obfuscates these deficiencies different players look at the game in different ways, so don't ignore the possibility of insight from anyone this is particularly relevant in doubles - ego is by far the most problematic thing in social dynamics between teammates work ethic is important for improvement at anything and is one of the most common deficiencies in melee players ego can damage your work ethic because of complacency and arrogance you might have been able to do 100 perfect ledgedashes last week, so you feel like you don't need to practice it anymore reliable tech skill comes at the price of eternal vigilance don't neglect practicing your bread and butter "because you're already good at it" how many hours do you think armada and m2k have spent comboing cpus? yet they still beat up cpus before getting on stage work ethic doesn't just mean practicing tech skill - it means maintaining the same fire you had when you were getting wrecked by your rival month after month if you lost to someone for years, then beat them week after week, it's easy to fall into complacency regardless of how good you are, you still need to go to tournaments and work on implementing new things the beauty of melee is that there is no skillcap - we should all strive to implement new things and polish our gameplay until the end of days don't tell yourself that after you lose a friendly to an arcadian that you would have won if it were tournament think about what you can learn from the game you just played don't john to protect your ego it's easy to attribute losing to factors outside of your control but factors outside your control are just that - outside your control hence, it's pointless to focus on them, because your own deficiencies are within your realm of influence ego makes you isolate yourself from situations that potentially damage it we all have friends who do disproportionately well against us for what our supposed respective skill levels are most of us hate playing these people - our egos hate that we do worse than we feel we should the fact is that these are people you should actively seek out to play - their playstyle exploits weaknesses in your own ego makes us want to avoid situations where we can get upset in tournament, or even avoid giving someone a runback after beating them don't avoid matches because you "have nothing to prove" don't seek out matches because you have to prove something for the sake of your ego to improve as rapidly as possible, you should play as much as possible against players who can potentially beat you expectations for results are an understandable reality of being a competitor however, having your ego tied to these results can take you out of the moment our lives are the cumulation of a series of present moments - there is nothing you can do to change the past the present has a deterministic relationship to the future, such that the only way to affect the future is through the decisions we make in the present the future does not exist as anything except an intangible idea don't let your ego make you worry about intangible meaningless concerns when playing a tournament set, all your focus should be dedicated to: what your opponent is doing what they're likely to do what options are available to you to counter theirs this is the last time you want to have thoughts creeping in about results the easiest way to get upset by someone you "should" beat is to start thinking about: what people are going to say about you losing how losing will affect your power ranking how you should be winning how you are so much better than your opponent all of these thoughts are inextricably linked to your ego focus on the game and not perception of your skill learning to silence your ego and have stillness of mind will result in your performance being better and vastly more consistent accept feedback from all sources, regardless of skill level maintain work ethic even when you're winning don't john - focus on what you can control seek out players who exploit your weaknesses stay in the present moment during tournament sets focus on the game, not on results or perception

than difficult this is perhaps the most important challenge of all at nationals, especially evo, you get less warmup the ratio of setups to players is not very good at most nationals we should all make a point of lauding tournaments where it's actually easy to get friendlies in (particularly with smashladder being a frequent side event) you often stand around for almost half an hour between matches, doing nothing, as all the setups are occupied for tournament matches then you have to sit down and immediately play your best if you sd or get shine spiked twice in the first game, that's likely to be the set suggestion: put special effort into staying in the zone between games many of us are normally social at tournaments, but at nationals, you might want to save socializing for after your pool is done focus on your upcoming match and what your goals for the day are in terms of execution and gameplan losing in the upper bracket at nationals sucks at locals, it's often a boon to lose early - you get to line up your opponents, get momentum, and cruise all the way through the tournament at nationals, you don't get to line up your opponents the same way you still wait a lot - pool waves hours apart and have to play over different days you have to play way more matches for the same placing you have a crazy high chance of coming across some gimmick, novel playstyle, or playstyle counter for you only the last of which is likely to happen at a local and if you make it to the last day in the lower bracket, you're in for a rough time playing well in the morning is hard, especially if it's the day after traveling, when you obviously couldn't practice at locals and regionals, you often don't have to play well until the sun is going down - the earlier matches are fluff it's incredibly rough when you have to wake up day 2 or day 3 at a national and your first match of the day is against an opponent who's better than you a lot of the time these are the most fun people to play - people who you can beat at your best but who will destroy you at your worst often, these players make you rise up to the challenge and make you play your best but if it's before noon and you're groggy from messed up sleep, a crazy night before, or just not being a morning person, you're probably just going to get run over find some kind of morning routine to ameliorate this gamers generally are night owls, so if you can learn to play your best in the morning, you'll have a huge advantage locals test some completely different skills endurance is a personal strength for some, and an all-day grind which starts with everyone and ends with one final winner is a format where some players thrive example - redbull g&g: lost to a relatively unknown arcadian quite badly early in the tournament. played awful. but the tournament reset everyone in the forsaken bracket to be in a new bracket with no losses, so didn't need to play very well until 7pm. it wasn't until lr2 in the forsaken bracket that play actually started improving. after grinding through a hangover and fatigue with the help of a ton of caffeine, finally found the groove grinding through your subpar play and finding your footing when you need to is unlikely to happen at a national though it's possible if you are trying to get through r2 pools at 6 or 8pm it's easier to prepare for brackets at locals nationals release brackets and pools far in advance, but watching videos or asking people what character your opponents play isn't the same when you go to locals, you know every relevant player's style, character, and character counterpicks example scenario: r1 pool wf opponent is a "pretty good marth." dumpster him game 1, slack a bit game 2 and let him edge you out on his counterpick, then pick fd game 3. he switches to falco. well fuck. no one told you he played falco. maybe there are no videos of him playing falco anywhere. you might just be in the lower bracket for the rest of the tournament these situations rarely come up at locals you're less likely to come across some gimmick strategy you haven't faced before maybe no one has ever planked against you. maybe you didn't know pikachu wrecks your character on fd because you didn't realize how busted his chaingrab is these are the kinds of things you'll learn after one exposure at a local eventually the pool of people who rely on such tactics and the potential new things for them to exploit dries up in your region at nationals, the odds of someone having some trick to edge out one game is much higher obnoxious crowds are scarcely a problem at locals even if people get rowdy in your region, it's pretty unlikely that someone is going to have their group of 10 friends behind them heckling you ever played against anyone from az or pittsburgh? ever play in a crew battle? it's hard locals really don't prepare you for the rowdiness and spotlight that come out at nationals someone who's top 20 in the world in a silent venue but not top 100 when getting heckled is not a bad player but given the environment at nationals, this is actually a possibility, and in current scene, we might never appreciate that player's skill because we might never see it manifest when the spotlight is there if you feel that's you: listen to music or get an audio setup! nationals require: handling travel fatigue, multi-day consistency, limited warmup, morning performance, dealing with unknowns, crowd pressure locals reward: endurance, grinding through bad play, familiarity with opponents, consistent environment both are valid tests of skill, just different ones prepare specifically for the format you're attending
